questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between a plain autoencoder and a VAE with respect to generation?
options: A VAE uses convolutional layers; an autoencoder uses fully connected layers
A VAE encoder outputs a distribution over the latent space; an autoencoder encodes to a single deterministic point
A VAE uses a larger bottleneck dimension than an autoencoder
A plain autoencoder supports sampling by using a Gaussian prior
questions.explanation: The key distinction is that a VAE encoder outputs (mu, sigma), parameterizing a distribution q(z|x). An autoencoder maps x to a fixed vector z with no probabilistic structure, so arbitrary points sampled from the code space decode to noise.

questions.question: What does the reparameterization trick accomplish in a VAE?
options: It replaces the KL term with a simpler L2 penalty
It rewrites the stochastic sample z as mu + sigma * eps so gradients can flow through the sampling operation
It converts the continuous latent into discrete tokens for transformer modeling
It forces the posterior to match a uniform distribution
questions.explanation: Sampling from q(z|x) is not differentiable, but writing z = mu + sigma * eps (eps ~ N(0,I)) makes z a deterministic function of the parameters plus pure noise, allowing gradients to flow through mu and sigma during backpropagation.

questions.question: In the VAE ELBO, what role does the KL divergence term play?
options: It measures pixel-wise reconstruction accuracy
It pushes the approximate posterior q(z|x) toward the prior N(0, I), shaping the latent space
It replaces the reconstruction loss when the decoder is Gaussian
It prevents the decoder weights from growing too large
questions.explanation: The KL term KL[q(z|x) || N(0,I)] regularizes the code space by pulling the encoder's distribution toward the prior. Without it the code space is unstructured and arbitrary prior samples decode to noise.

questions.question: What is posterior collapse in a VAE, and what causes it?
options: The decoder outputs all-zero images; caused by too-small learning rate
The encoder ignores the input and maps every x to the prior; caused by the KL term dominating the loss
The latent dimensions shrink to zero over training; caused by large batch sizes
The decoder produces blurry images; caused by an MSE reconstruction loss
questions.explanation: Posterior collapse occurs when the KL penalty pushes q(z|x) all the way to the prior N(0,I) regardless of input x. The decoder then receives no information and must hallucinate. Common fixes include beta-annealing and free-bits.

questions.question: Why do VAEs produce blurry samples even after successful training?
options: The KL term is too small to shape the latent space properly
The Gaussian decoder likelihood penalizes the mean of plausible outputs, which is a fuzzy average
The reparameterization trick introduces too much noise at inference
Posterior collapse causes the decoder to ignore the latent
questions.explanation: A Gaussian (MSE) decoder is Bayes-optimal for the mean of the output distribution. The mean of many plausible images of a digit is a blurry digit. Discrete decoders (VQ-VAE) or stacking diffusion on the latents (Stable Diffusion) are the standard fixes.

questions.question: In Stable Diffusion and similar latent-diffusion models, what is the primary role of the VAE?
options: To generate images directly from text prompts
To compress images into a lower-dimensional latent space where diffusion is run
To score the quality of generated samples during training
To provide text embeddings for cross-attention conditioning
questions.explanation: Stable Diffusion's VAE compresses 512x512 images to 64x64x4 latents (a 48x spatial reduction). Diffusion runs in this compact latent space, making training and inference far cheaper than pixel-space diffusion.
